book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook builds the measures one from another (GDP, add NFIA for GNP, subtract depreciation for NDP and NNP, then factor cost vs market price) and only later says which is national income and which is used for comparison. Here the definitions are a quick parade (the details were taught in earlier videos) and the real teaching is two judging questions: round 1 'which gives the truest national income' crowns NNP at factor cost, round 2 'which compares countries' eliminates by a rule (depreciation) and then by three reasons. Ordering by purpose works for revision: the learner leaves knowing when to use which measure, not just four formulas.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each measure gets one turn (definition plus what it reveals: strength, dependence, efficiency, purity); then the topic is cut by purpose, one round per question a measure must answer, and the losers are removed by a rule or by numbered reasons.

opening.what: Says the last few videos covered GDP, GNP, NDP and NNP in detail; today they compete, and the winner is the one that gives the most accurate national income.

moves.concept: the four measures as contestants (contest frame)
moves.what: Earlier videos covered the four measures; this one is a revision contest.

moves.concept: the four measures as contestants (contest frame)
moves.what: Announces a competition between the four with a winning rule (most accurate value of national income). New move flavour: a contest frame with a judging question.

moves.concept: GDP: output inside the border, internal strength, jobs
moves.what: 'Shuruaat karte hain GDP se': each turn opens with a signpost to the next measure.

moves.concept: GDP: output inside the border, internal strength, jobs
moves.what: GDP is the money value of all goods and services produced inside a country's geographical boundary.

moves.concept: GDP: output inside the border, internal strength, jobs
moves.what: 'Yaani' GDP shows the internal strength of the economy; 'iska matlab' its growth tells whether more jobs are being created.

moves.concept: GNP: output of residents anywhere, internal and external strength
moves.what: GNP adds up what the country's residents produce, in India or outside it.

moves.concept: GNP: output of residents anywhere, internal and external strength
moves.what: So GNP shows both internal and external strength: whether we depend more on other countries or they on us.

moves.concept: NDP: GDP minus depreciation, read as efficiency
moves.what: NDP is GDP minus depreciation.

moves.concept: NDP: GDP minus depreciation, read as efficiency
moves.what: Depreciation falls only when R&D improves, so NDP over time shows whether the economy's efficiency is rising or falling (a doubtful link; flag).

moves.concept: NNP: GNP minus depreciation; NNP at factor cost = national income (NI)
moves.what: NNP is GNP minus depreciation, then unpacked again in plain words (residents at home or abroad, add their output, remove depreciation).

moves.concept: NNP: GNP minus depreciation; NNP at factor cost = national income (NI)
moves.what: Because it counts only our residents' output and removes depreciation, it is the purest form of national income; therefore NNP at factor cost gets the title and is written NI.

moves.concept: NNP: GNP minus depreciation; NNP at factor cost = national income (NI)
moves.what: GDP, GNP and NDP also measure national income, but if one must be called national income it is NNP.

moves.concept: per capita income: nominal and real
moves.what: Divide NNP at factor cost by total population for nominal per capita income; remove inflation up to the base year for real per capita income.

moves.concept: per capita income: nominal and real
moves.what: Real per capita income is the appropriate way to measure economic growth.

moves.concept: per capita income: nominal and real
moves.what: Round 1 result restated: NNP won the national income title.

moves.concept: round 2 rule: no depreciation-based measure for cross-country comparison
moves.what: Announces round 2: which measure can compare economic growth of different countries.

moves.concept: round 2 rule: no depreciation-based measure for cross-country comparison
moves.what: Rule: measures that use depreciation are out, because each government sets its own depreciation rate and rates differ; so NNP and NDP leave, and the contest is GNP vs GDP, which GDP wins.

moves.concept: reason 1: dual citizenship double counting in GNP
moves.what: It is important to know why GNP cannot be used; there are three main reasons.

moves.concept: reason 1: dual citizenship double counting in GNP
moves.what: 'Maan lijiye' a person is a citizen of X and Y and works in Z, producing Rs 100 of goods; both X and Y count the Rs 100.

moves.concept: reason 1: dual citizenship double counting in GNP
moves.what: So dual citizenship brings a double counting problem into GNP (doubtful claim; flag).

moves.concept: reason 2: NFIA depends on fluctuating exchange rates
moves.what: GNP = GDP + NFIA; NFIA depends on the exchange rate; exchange rates keep fluctuating; so GNP fluctuates and comparison gets hard.

moves.concept: reason 3: GNP can rise while GDP and jobs fall
moves.what: GDP moves with jobs; if GDP is down, unemployment is high.

moves.concept: reason 3: GNP can rise while GDP and jobs fall
moves.what: If NFIA rises so fast that GNP still grows, would we say the economy is growing? Answered at once: 'bilkul nahin'.

moves.concept: reason 3: GNP can rise while GDP and jobs fall
moves.what: The economy is shrinking but GNP shows growth, so GNP can give misleading figures.

moves.concept: verdict: GDP compares countries' growth
moves.what: These are the reasons GDP, not GNP, is used to compare growth across countries.

examples.what: The four measures are contestants in a bodybuilding-style competition with two rounds and a winner per round.
examples.carries: measures judged by purpose: which is national income, which compares countries

examples.what: A dual citizen of X and Y works in Z and produces Rs 100; both X and Y add the Rs 100 to their GNP.
examples.carries: double counting when GNP is summed across countries (doubtful as stated)

examples.what: GDP falls and unemployment rises, yet NFIA rises fast enough that GNP grows.
examples.carries: why GNP can mislead about growth

closing.what: One line says these are the reasons GDP is used rather than GNP to compare countries, then the playlist plug; no recap of round 1 and no table of the four measures.

narration.density: About 25 terms (GDP, geographical boundary, monetary value, internal strength, GNP, residents, external strength, dependence, NDP, depreciation, R&D, efficiency, NNP, purest form, factor cost, national income, NI, per capita income, nominal and real PCI, base year, inflation, dual citizenship, double counting, NFIA, foreign exchange rate) in about 390 s, roughly 4 per minute. Dense for a first lesson but it is framed as revision of earlier videos; the definitions parade fast and the comparison rounds slow down well.

talmel_summary: Picture and voice land together on most tiles, but in round 1 the fit is mostly 'heading repeats the spoken word' (INTERNAL STRENGTH, EFFICIENCY, PUREST FORM): the stage, contestant and card change on the measure's name, and the meaning lives in paragraph cards. The fit becomes real showing in round 2 and the reasons: crosses on the two depreciation-based measures, 'VS' on 'muqabla', a person doing the splits on 'do countries ka nagrik', two arrows claiming one Rs 100, and red/green arrows on the parts of GNP = GDP + NFIA as the cause chain is spoken. Transitions often run a few seconds ahead of speech (next contestant walks in ~6 s before NDP is named). Two transcript gaps (54-61 s, 175-180 s) fall between tiles.

voice.notes: About 179 words per minute, brisk, flat and even; a recap pace. Every turn opens with the same signpost ('chaliye baat karte hain next measure ki') and every idea ends with 'to iska matlab yah hua ki', which makes the structure easy to hear but repetitive. The contest frame is carried by words like 'competition', 'vijeta', 'muqabla', 'bahar kar diya'. One rhetorical question with an instant 'bilkul nahin'. Rs 100 is read as 'worth rupees 100'. No pauses for the learner to guess the winner.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a small economy for a year: 3 factories inside India (one foreign-owned, sending Rs 50 profit home), 2 Indians working abroad earning Rs 80, machines that wear out by Rs 100. For each contestant (GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP) the player drags items into or out of that contestant's basket.
game_ideas.process_happens: The basket total counts up (GDP 1000, GNP 1030, NDP 900, NNP 930); an item crossing the border flies along the map, and the wear-and-tear chunk breaks off the machines when subtracted.
game_ideas.win: All four baskets correct; the player then crowns one with the national income sash and must pick NNP at factor cost.
game_ideas.lose: Putting the foreign-owned factory's profit into GNP makes the coins fly out of India on the map and the GNP basket flashes; forgetting depreciation in NDP leaves the worn machine glowing red.
game_ideas.concept: NNP: GNP minus depreciation; NNP at factor cost = national income (NI)

game_ideas.player_does: Judges round 2: two countries with identical factories are compared; the player picks which measure to rank them by, then moves two sliders: each government's depreciation rule and the exchange rate.
game_ideas.process_happens: With NDP or NNP the ranking flips when the depreciation rule slider moves even though nothing real changed; with GNP it flips when the exchange rate moves; with GDP it stays put.
game_ideas.win: Choose GDP and explain the flip seen with each other measure.
game_ideas.lose: Choosing NNP or GNP and moving a slider swaps the winner on the podium with no change in factories, showing why the rule bans them.
game_ideas.concept: round 2 rule: no depreciation-based measure for cross-country comparison

game_ideas.player_does: Watches a year in which a factory closes and remittances rise; must set each arrow (GDP, jobs, NFIA, GNP) up or down and then answer 'is the economy growing?'.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each arrow set right makes that part of GNP = GDP + NFIA change colour; the jobs counter drops as GDP falls while GNP's bar still rises.
game_ideas.win: All arrows right and answer 'no, it is shrinking; GNP misleads'.
game_ideas.lose: Answering 'growing' because GNP rose shows the queue of jobless workers behind the green GNP bar.
game_ideas.concept: reason 3: GNP can rise while GDP and jobs fall

notes_questions.q: GDP, GNP, NDP aur NNP mein kya farq hai? Border, residents aur depreciation ke hisaab se table banaiye.
GDP ko 'internal strength' aur GNP ko 'internal + external strength' kyon kaha gaya?
NNP at factor cost ko hi National Income (NI) kyon kehte hain?
Per capita income kaise nikalte hain, aur nominal aur real PCI mein kya farq hai?
Alag-alag deshon ki growth compare karte waqt NDP aur NNP kyon nahi lete?
GNP ko countries compare karne ke liye kyon nahi lete? Teen kaaran likhiye.
Agar GDP gire aur NFIA tezi se badhe, to GNP kya dikhayega aur kyon yeh misleading hai?

checks_learned: No verdict mark (tick, crown, sash) may appear before the narration gives the verdict; here the tick on NNP shows at the start of a contest whose result comes 2.5 minutes later.
When a definition is spoken as a formula (NDP = GDP - depreciation), the formula must be on screen, not only a descriptive paragraph.
Key words must match between screen and voice and between cards (residents vs citizens for GNP and NNP).
When the narration announces N reasons or steps, a visible counter with N slots must be on screen and advance on each 'pehla / doosra / teesra' (worked here with the 3-step podium).

Absolute economic claims ('directly proportional', 'cannot be used') should be flagged for a fact check; e.g. GNI per capita is widely used to classify countries, and national accounts count residents, not citizens.
Definition cards over about 25 words on a character turn should be split: one picture of the rule (border, resident abroad, wear and tear) plus a 3-5 word heading.
A transcript gap over 4 s at the start of a new idea (175-180 s here) should be flagged for re-transcription before talmel is judged.

teaching_best.why: Turning four look-alike measures into contestants with a judging question gives a revision video a goal; each round has one question and one winner.
Round 2 starts with a stated rule and its reason, then applies it: two contestants are out before any detail, which is how an examiner eliminates options.
A 'maan lijiye' case with one person and Rs 100 makes the abstract objection to GNP concrete (even though the claim needs checking).
A what-if where the total rises while its main part and jobs fall, followed by an instant 'bilkul nahin': the learner feels why one number can mislead.

teaching_weak.why: The NNP tick in the opening tree gives away round 1's winner.
Claims depreciation falls only when R&D improves and that NDP shows R&D achievements; the link is doubtful and the efficiency reading is not explained.
'NNP at factor cost' is crowned without saying what factor cost means here (left to another video).
The dual-citizenship double counting reason is doubtful as stated; national accounts assign each person to one resident economy.
Ends on the verdict alone; no closing table of which measure is used for what.
